readings.title: A message pretending to be a delivery company
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents received a text saying that a parcel could not be delivered. The link requested card details for a small redelivery charge. The main obstacle was a payment request from an unverified sender. The message used urgent wording but gave no reliable order number. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a comparison with official delivery channels. Digital advisers showed residents how to open the known company site without using the message link. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the parcel claim could not be confirmed. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a clear warning and independent verification steps. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: urgent messages deserve a pause before payment. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a message pretending to be a delivery company, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Sharing photographs at a school event
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Parents took photographs at a school concert. A group chat later included images of children whose families had not agreed to public posting. The main obstacle was consent rules unclear to visitors. The event notice mentioned photography but did not separate private memories from online publication. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a review of event guidance and parent questions. Staff asked families what information they had received and checked the school policy. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a clear posting rule prevented confusion. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced signs that distinguish taking photos from publishing them. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: personal information can spread through ordinary habits. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in sharing photographs at a school event, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A password lesson for older users
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A digital-skills class taught password creation. Several participants wrote their new passwords on a shared worksheet left in the classroom. The main obstacle was practice that exposed real account details. The exercise had not explained that examples should be invented rather than taken from personal accounts. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review of training materials. Tutors checked every activity for moments when learners might reveal private information. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated fictional examples made the lesson safer. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced sample accounts and private take-home guidance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: security education must model safe behaviour. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a password lesson for older users, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A public computer after a form submission
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library visitor completed an online application on a shared computer. The next user could still see the previous page in the browser. The main obstacle was a session left open after the visitor departed. The computer returned to its home screen without signing out of the external service. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a supervised review of session endings. Library staff traced the steps and consulted its technology team about safe reset settings. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated closing the window was not always enough. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced automatic session clearing and a visible sign-out reminder. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: shared devices need clear privacy safeguards. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a public computer after a form submission, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning digital safety and personal information often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the community digital safety programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关数字安全与个人信息的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the digital safety team proposing a small improvement to the community digital safety programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community digital safety programme. People have noticed a payment request from an unverified sender, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
